lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: practical: investigate breathing in humans, including the release of carbon dioxide and the effect of exercise

primer.text: Breathing responds to demand, and the demand is measurable. This practical counts breaths per minute at rest and straight after exercise, then asks how reliably the change can be attributed to the activity — which is where the CORMS checklist earns its keep.

modules.title: Counting the Change
sourceHeadings: Practical: The Effect of Age on Breathing
modules.opening: Participants of a similar age sit quietly for a minute and count their breaths — one inhale plus one exhale each. They then perform identical exercise, such as running on the spot, and count again immediately. The difference between the two counts is the change in breathing rate, and repeating across participants gives a mean worth comparing.
keyPoints: Breathing rate is counted as breaths per minute, one breath being an inhale and an exhale.
A resting count comes first, then the same exercise for everyone.
The count repeats immediately after exercise stops.
Change in breathing rate equals the after-exercise rate minus the resting rate.
Repeats across participants allow a mean to be calculated.

low.restatement: Two counts and their difference measure what exercise did to breathing.
low.analogy: A stopwatch on a car before and after a hill: the delta is the hill's cost.
low.examPointer: Write the change as a subtraction — after minus before — in method answers.

medium.restatement: Exercise raises breathing rate and depth to serve the muscles' demand.
medium.analogy: A delivery service adding vans and bigger vans when orders surge.
medium.examPointer: Give the biological reason — oxygen demand and carbon dioxide clearance — not just the observation.

modules.title: Limitations and Fixes
modules.opening: Honest practicals admit their weak spots. Participant variation is hard to control; exercise effort differs between people; counting breaths is error-prone because rates shift fast; and the room itself — temperature, air quality, nerves — leaks into the numbers. Each weakness has a standard fix worth quoting.
keyPoints: Fitness, lifestyle and health vary between participants and cannot all be controlled.
Motivation and ability make exercise intensity differ between people.
Counting errors arise because breathing rate changes quickly after exercise.
A controlled exercise, such as step-ups at a set pace, pins the intensity down.
Counting for a fixed short spell and scaling up reduces the timing error.

low.restatement: Every measurement weakness has a named fix — learn them as pairs.
low.analogy: A survey with sloppy handwriting: standardise the form and the mess shrinks.
low.examPointer: Quote the limitation and its solution together; one without the other scores half.

medium.restatement: Set-pace exercise, immediate short counts, and identical indoor conditions — the three fixes.
medium.analogy: A kitchen timer strategy: measure the freshest interval and scale it to the recipe.
medium.examPointer: Write limitation then solution in the same sentence for full marks.

glossary.definition: The number of breaths taken per minute; one breath is an inhale plus an exhale.
The practical checklist: Change, Organism, Repeat, Measure, Same.
The average of repeated measurements, used to smooth individual variation.
